transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, I guess I'm here because... we recently did a little updating in our master bathroom. You know how it is, the old fixtures were from the nineties, that awful shiny brass color? My husband finally agreed to change them out, which was a whole ordeal because he wanted to go to three different hardware stores just to compare prices on towel racks. Men, right? 

Anyway, we put in this new, much brighter mirror—it has those built-in LED lights around the edge. And ever since we put that in, I just... I keep noticing that the skin around my cheeks and my jaw looks really uneven. Or kind of saggy to me? It just looks bad. I keep pointing it out, but my husband says he can't really see what I'm talking about. But honestly, he also didn't even notice when I completely reorganized all the client files at the law firm where I work last week, so I don't know if he's the best judge of detail anyway. But yeah, it's just really bothering me how uneven my face looks in that light.
Do you find yourself thinking about the unevenness of your skin a lot throughout the day?

Well, yeah, I guess I do think about it a fair bit. Most mornings now, I end up standing there checking my face from a few different angles in that new mirror, and I usually have to put on a little extra makeup before I leave for the courthouse. Which, by the way, the courthouse parking situation has been an absolute nightmare lately. They're doing all this construction on the east garage, so everyone is fighting for spots in the visitor lot. I had to park three blocks away on Tuesday, and I was carrying like four heavy binders for my boss, Mr. Davis. He’s been so stressed about this civil suit we're prepping for that he actually spilled coffee all over his tie right before a deposition. 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right, my skin. Yeah, I do think about it during the day. Like, when I'm at work, I catch myself comparing my face to the other women at the firm. And if Susan from HR brings out her phone to take casual pictures for the firm's monthly newsletter—which I swear nobody even reads except maybe the managing partner's wife, she's always replying all to the emails about it—I'll just kind of step out of the frame or avoid being in the pictures entirely if I'm not feeling okay about how my cheeks and jaw look. So, yeah, it definitely pops into my head.
Has your concern about the appearance of your skin affected your relationships with colleagues or your ability to perform your job?

Well, I still get my work done, thankfully. I mean, if I didn't, the whole office would probably fall apart. Mr. Davis can barely find his own stapler half the time, let alone file a motion without me. But... because of the extra time I spend getting ready in the morning, trying to fix how my skin looks, I have had to rush into the courthouse a few mornings lately. And rushing through the security line there is just awful. The main guard, Gary, he insists everyone takes off their shoes and belts even when the machine isn't beeping, which just backs up the whole line out the door. 

So yeah, I've been rushing. And I've actually missed the start of my evening yoga class more than once, too, because I was fussing with my makeup before leaving the house again. Which is so frustrating because the instructor, she locks the studio door right on the dot, and then you have to stand out in the chilly hallway listening to her weird pan-flute music until she lets the latecomers in. 

As for my relationships... I don't know, I guess I've also skipped out on a few casual photos at my book club and some community events lately. I just really didn't want to worry about how my face would look in the pictures. Especially at book club, where Mary always posts them straight to Facebook without even putting a filter on. Oh, and we're reading this new murder mystery right now that is just dragging on, I swear the detective in the book is completely clueless, I figured out who did it in chapter three. But anyway, yeah, I just try to stay out of the photos when I can so I don't have to stress about it.
Are you finding that your concerns about your skin are affecting any of your hobbies or activities that you enjoy doing alone?

Well, alone? I mean, I don't know that it really stops me from doing things by myself. Like, I still read a lot, obviously, even if that book club pick is a total dud right now. I usually read out on the back patio if the weather's nice. Oh, but the neighbors behind us just got this massive golden retriever puppy, and I swear that dog does nothing but bark at the fence line every time a squirrel even twitches. It's impossible to concentrate. My husband went over there to say something about it last weekend, but you know him, he probably just ended up talking to the guy about lawnmowers for twenty minutes and completely forgot why he went over in the first place. He’s obsessed with getting a riding mower even though our yard is barely a quarter acre. 

But, um... no, I guess if I'm just by myself, reading or gardening or whatever, I'm not really thinking about my skin or avoiding anything. It's mostly just when I have to be around other people or in pictures, you know?
Do you think other people notice the unevenness of your skin as much as you do?

Well, honestly, I don't think they do. I mean, my husband definitely doesn't. He says he can't really see what I'm talking about when I point it out to him. But then again, he also didn't notice when I painted the entire downstairs half-bath a completely different shade of blue last month. I spent all weekend taping the trim and moving the vanity, and he walked in on Sunday night and just asked if we were out of hand soap. Typical, right? 

But anyway, yeah, I'm really only here because ever since we put in that new, brighter bathroom mirror—the one with the LED lights around the edge that I ordered online, which took forever to ship, by the way, they kept saying it was out for delivery and then it wouldn't show up—I just keep noticing that the skin around my cheeks and jaw looks so uneven. Or kind of saggy, maybe? I don't know, it just bothers me. But no, I guess my husband doesn't see it as much as I do.
Do you think your skin actually looks uneven, or is it just that you feel like it should look better?

Well, I mean... I think it actually looks uneven? But then again, maybe I just feel like it should look better, I don't know. It's hard to tell what's real and what isn't with all the filters and things people use now. 

Like, I was at the dentist on Tuesday for my six-month cleaning, and Dr. Miller still has magazines from like 2019 in his waiting room. I told his receptionist, Brenda, that they really ought to update them, especially since half the recipes are torn out of the Good Housekeeping ones. Brenda is so sweet, though, she's been working that front desk for twenty years and she always remembers that I hate the cherry-flavored polishing paste. Cherry flavoring always tastes exactly like that awful cough syrup we had to take as kids, don't you think? I don't know who actually chooses that flavor on purpose. My husband probably would, he loves anything cherry. 

But anyway, I was flipping through one of those old magazines, and all the women in there just have this completely flawless, smooth skin. Not a bump or a shadow anywhere. So maybe I'm just looking at things like that and expecting my own face to look better than it naturally does? I really couldn't tell you for sure. I just know it bothers me when I look in that new mirror.
Is there something specific about the unevenness of your skin that bothers you, or is it more that you wish your skin looked perfect?

Well, I don't know if I'd say I need it to be *perfect*. Perfect is a strong word, right? Like, my sister-in-law, Susan, she expects everything to be perfect. You should see her at Thanksgiving. If the turkey isn't carved exactly the way she saw it on some cooking show, she practically ruins the whole dinner complaining about it. Last year, she made my brother drive to three different grocery stores on Thanksgiving morning just to find a specific brand of cranberry sauce, because the one he bought wasn't the "right" kind. I told her, Susan, it all tastes the same once it's on the plate, but you can't tell her anything. She’s just so particular. 

But for me and my skin... I'm not sure. I don't think it's about being perfect. It's just... I don't know, it's just that I see it in that mirror, and it bothers me. I can't really put my finger on exactly what it is, honestly. It just doesn't look right to me.
Is it the specific unevenness and sagging of your skin that bothers you, or is it more about wanting to have smoother skin in general?

I mean, I don't really know if there's a difference? I haven't really thought about it like that. I guess everyone wants smoother skin in general, right? 

Like, at the law firm where I work, we have this fancy hand lotion in the women's restroom. The managing partner's wife, Mrs. Davis, she buys it in bulk from some little boutique out in Sedona and has it shipped directly to the office. It smells like lavender and eucalyptus, which she says is supposed to be calming for the staff, but honestly, it just makes my hands so incredibly greasy when I'm trying to sort through deposition transcripts. Have you ever tried to flip through hundreds of pages of legal documents with greasy fingers? It's completely impossible. You just end up leaving little oily thumbprints on everything, and I'm always the one who has to organize the exhibits for trial, so I really can't be getting lotion all over the evidence binders. Mr. Davis would absolutely have a fit if I handed him a smudged file in the middle of a hearing. 

But anyway, with my face... I really couldn't tell you if it's the specific sagging or just wanting it to be smoother overall. I just look in that new bathroom mirror and I don't like what I see. I'm not really sure how to separate the two things, honestly.

Is it the thought of having this specific unevenness and sagging that bothers you, or would you feel better if your skin just looked generally smoother and more even, even if it wasn't perfectly flawless?

Well, I guess I'd feel better if it was smoother, but it's just... I can't stop focusing on it. I’m really only here because ever since we put in that brighter bathroom mirror, I just keep noticing that the skin around my cheeks and jaw looks uneven or kind of saggy to me. 

And it's so frustrating because my husband says he can’t really see what I’m talking about. But then again, he doesn't notice a lot of things. Like last weekend, I spent three hours cleaning out the garage, organizing all his tools into those little plastic bins I bought at Target—the ones with the clear lids so you can actually see what's inside without opening every single one. I even labeled them with my label maker. I love that label maker, it's the Brother P-touch, the one with the different fonts? I used the cursive one for the gardening supplies because I thought it looked nice. Anyway, he walked right past all of it to get his golf clubs and didn't say a single word. Not a peep! I had to actually point out the bins to him on Sunday night, and he just said, "Oh, looks good, honey." Three hours of my Saturday, gone! 

But yeah, the mirror... it's just so bright. Every time I go in there to wash my face or brush my teeth, my eyes just go right to my cheeks and my jawline. I just see all these little uneven spots and that sagging, and it just bothers me so much, even if he says he doesn't see it.
Is it the presence of this specific unevenness and sagging that bothers you, or would any imperfection in your skin be bothersome to you?

I mean, I don't really know if *any* imperfection would bother me, because I haven't really thought about it like that. It's just this specific thing right now. Like I said, I'm really only here because ever since we put in that brighter bathroom mirror, I keep noticing that the skin around my cheeks and jaw looks uneven or kind of saggy to me. 

And mirrors are so tricky, aren't they? Like the ones in department store dressing rooms. Have you ever noticed how some of them make you look completely washed out, and others make you look like you haven't slept in a week? I was at Macy's last month trying to find a dress for my nephew's graduation—he just finished his undergrad at Arizona State, which is great, but honestly, I don't know what he's going to do with a degree in philosophy. My brother is completely stressed out about it because he's paying the student loans. Anyway, I tried on this navy blue wrap dress, and the lighting in that dressing room was just atrocious. It was this harsh, fluorescent overhead light, and it made every single shadow on my face look ten times worse. I actually left the dress right there on the hook and walked out because I felt so bad about how I looked in it. 

But with my bathroom mirror, it's just... that's where I see it every single day. The unevenness and the sagging. It just really bothers me, even though my husband says he can’t really see what I’m talking about.
Is it the fact that you see this specific unevenness and sagging in the mirror that bothers you, or would you feel self-conscious about any flaw in your skin, no matter how small?

I honestly don't know. I mean, it's hard to say if every single little thing would bother me, because I'm really just focused on this one specific thing right now. It's just the sagging and the unevenness that I see. 

Talking about tiny flaws, though, it's funny you word it like that, because at work, I'm the one who has to catch all the tiny flaws in the contracts. You would not believe the typos these junior associates make. We have this new kid, Tyler—he just passed the bar, went to Georgetown, so you'd think he'd know how to use a spell checker, right? But last Tuesday, he misspelled "subpoena" three times in a single motion. Three times! And I'm the one who has to catch it before it goes to the judge. If I didn't have my red pens, I swear the whole firm would just fall apart. I actually buy my own pens for the office, the Pilot G2s in the 0.5 millimeter point, because the office manager only orders those cheap bulk ballpoint ones that skip when you write fast. And when you're trying to mark up a fifty-page document, you really need a pen that flows well, you know? 

But, um... sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, my face. Yeah, I don't really know about other flaws or being self-conscious about everything. It's really just the sagging around my jaw that I see in that bright mirror that's bothering me right now.
Would you feel better about your skin if the specific unevenness and sagging you see were addressed, or is it more about having flawless skin in general?

I really think it's just this specific issue. Like I keep saying, I don't need to look like a magazine cover or have completely perfect skin. It’s just... ever since that new, bright mirror went up in the bathroom, my eyes just go straight to my jawline and my cheeks, and that uneven, saggy look is all I can focus on. Even if my husband completely swears he doesn't notice a thing. 

Which, speaking of that mirror, we actually got it on clearance at Home Depot because we were updating the bathroom fixtures. I originally wanted brushed nickel for the lights above it, but he insisted on matte black because he saw it on one of those home renovation shows. Have you ever watched those? They make it look so easy, like they just snap their fingers and a whole room is remodeled. In reality, the contractor left drywall dust all over my hallway for two weeks. I was vacuuming constantly. I have one of those cordless Dysons—the V10, I think? It’s incredibly convenient for stairs, but honestly, if you put it on the max suction setting, the battery dies in like fifteen minutes. You can barely finish a single room before you have to plug it back into the wall dock, which is just a terrible design flaw if you ask me. 

But anyway... what were we saying? Right, the skin. Yeah, I don't need totally flawless skin everywhere. I'd definitely feel a hundred times better if just this one specific sagging problem was addressed, because it's driving me crazy every time I turn on those bright lights in the bathroom.
Would you still be concerned about your skin if the unevenness and sagging around your jawline were the only imperfections you had, but they were still present?

I mean, yes, definitely. Like I think I've been saying, it wouldn't matter if the rest of my face was completely perfect. I'd still be just as upset about this one thing. It all goes back to that bright bathroom mirror we put in. Ever since we installed it, I just keep noticing how the skin around my cheeks and jaw looks so uneven and kind of saggy. And I know I keep bringing this up, but it's just so frustrating because my husband swears he can't really see what I'm talking about. 

But honestly, Dave’s observation skills are just terrible anyway. Typical man, right? Just last weekend I asked him to grab the minced garlic from the fridge, and he stood there with the door open for five whole minutes staring into the abyss. It was right there on the second shelf next to the butter! He was like, 'We're out of garlic, honey.' I had to walk over, reach right past him, and hand it to him. And don't even get me started on the time I got my hair done with caramel lowlights and he didn't notice for three days. Three days! My sister noticed the second I walked into her house for Sunday dinner. We always do Sunday dinner at her place because she has the bigger dining room, which is nice, though honestly her roast beef is always a little dry. She cooks it at 400 degrees the whole time instead of turning it down, which just ruins the meat... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, if it was the only imperfection. Yeah, I'd still be concerned. Because that sagging is what I see every single time I turn the lights on in that bathroom, whether Dave sees it or not.
Would your concern about your skin go away if you couldn't see the unevenness and sagging in the mirror, or would you still want to address it even if you couldn't see it?

I mean, if I couldn't see it at all? I guess maybe the concern would go away, yeah. Because honestly, the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you is that ever since we put in that brighter bathroom mirror, I just keep noticing it. It's just right there—the skin around my cheeks and jaw looking all uneven and saggy to me, even if Dave still swears he can't see what I'm talking about. 

But speaking of seeing things, I actually just had to get new reading glasses last month. I was getting these awful headaches from staring at PDF contracts on my monitor all day. The optometrist—Dr. Lin, she was so sweet—said my prescription hadn't even changed much, it was just digital eye strain. Of course, the sales lady out front still tried to upsell me on that blue-light blocking coating for the lenses. It’s like an extra sixty dollars! I told her, I'm already paying out of pocket because our firm's vision insurance is an absolute joke. They switched us to this new discount plan in January to save the partners some money, and the network is so tiny now. You practically have to drive an hour just to find an in-network eye doctor. Don't even get me started on the new dental plan. My hygienist said they barely cover a standard cleaning anymore, which is ridiculous because preventive care is exactly what keeps people out of the dentist's chair for the expensive stuff, you know? 

But, um, anyway. Sorry, I lost my train of thought. Oh, right, if I couldn't see the sagging. Yeah, I probably wouldn't be as upset. It really is just that bright mirror showing me every little saggy, uneven spot on my jaw that brought me in here to begin with.
Would you still be bothered by the unevenness and sagging if you couldn't see it in the mirror?

I think I actually just mentioned this, but no, if I couldn't see it, it probably wouldn't bother me at all. Out of sight, out of mind, I guess. It’s funny you’re asking me that again, though, because it totally reminds me of Mr. Gable at the law firm where I work. He’s one of the senior partners I assist, and he will literally ask me to pull the exact same case files three times in a single morning because he completely forgets he already asked me. 

And I have to walk all the way down to the physical records room every time, which is absolutely freezing, by the way. The building management controls the thermostat for the whole floor, and they must keep the basement at like sixty degrees. I have to keep this thick, ugly wool cardigan draped over my desk chair just to go down there. My coworker Sheila actually bought one of those little ceramic space heaters for under her desk, but building security came by and confiscated it last week. They said it was a fire hazard. Which is just hilarious to me, because the microwave in our breakroom literally sparks if you run it for more than two minutes, and nobody seems to care about that hazard. Someone tried to heat up a frozen lasagna in there on Tuesday and the whole hallway smelled like burnt plastic for the rest of the afternoon. 

But, um... wait, didn't you just ask me that? Sorry, my brain is all over the place today. But yeah, if I couldn't see the unevenness in the mirror, I really don't think I'd be worrying about it.
Is your concern about the unevenness and sagging of your skin driven more by the fact that it's a specific flaw you notice, or by a general desire to have perfect skin?

I mean, it's definitely just this specific thing. I don't need to look like a supermodel or have flawless porcelain skin or anything. It's really just... well, like I said, it's that brighter bathroom mirror we put in. Ever since we installed it, I just keep noticing how the skin around my cheeks and jaw looks so uneven and saggy to me. Even though Dave says he can't see it, it's just this one specific spot that drives me crazy. 

Which, honestly, getting that mirror installed was a whole ordeal in itself. We hired this contractor, Gary, who was highly recommended by my neighbor Susan. But Gary was completely useless. He said it would take two days, and it took him two and a half weeks! And he left his tools everywhere. I stepped on a screwdriver in my bare feet one morning. I almost called out of work because it hurt so bad, but we were right in the middle of a massive discovery phase for the Henderson case, and I knew Mr. Gable would be totally lost without me there to organize the exhibits. Susan felt so bad she baked me a batch of her famous lemon bars to apologize for recommending him. They were actually a little too tart, to be honest. She uses Meyer lemons, which I think are just a bit much, but I ate them anyway to be polite. 

But, um, yeah. It's not about having perfect skin everywhere. It's just that one specific saggy, uneven area on my jaw that I see in that darn mirror.

Is it the fact that you perceive this specific unevenness and sagging as a flaw that bothers you, or would you feel the same way if you simply wanted smoother skin without noticing any particular imperfections?

I'm sorry, I feel like you're asking me the same thing over and over. I mean, it's definitely the specific flaw. I don't care about just having generally smooth skin, it's that I see this sagging and unevenness right here on my jaw, and it bothers me. If I didn't see it, I wouldn't care. 

It's actually kind of like how Dave is with his car. He doesn't care if the whole car is perfectly clean, but if there's one tiny scratch on the bumper, he loses his mind. He spent three hours in the driveway last Saturday with this special buffing compound he ordered online just to fix a scrape that I couldn't even see. And he missed the start of the college football game he'd been talking about all week! He was so mad because his team fumbled on the very first drive, and he had to watch the replay instead of seeing it live. He actually knocked over his iced tea on the coffee table when he saw the replay. I had to rush in with the carpet cleaner before it stained the rug. It's a light beige rug, which was a terrible idea with a golden retriever, honestly. Buster sheds everywhere, and his muddy paws... 

But anyway, yeah. I just don't like this specific saggy spot. I don't need perfect skin.
Would you still want to address the unevenness and sagging if you didn't perceive it as a flaw, but rather just wanted smoother skin?

I feel like we're going in circles here. I really do. I just... I don't know how else to say it. If I didn't see it as a flaw, I wouldn't care. I don't just want smoother skin for the fun of it. It's the sagging that bothers me. 

Honestly, this repetition is making me feel like I'm back in court with Mr. Gable when he's cross-examining a witness. He does this exact same thing! He'll ask the witness the same question five different ways just to see if they slip up. Last month, we had this expert witness, a structural engineer, and Mr. Gable just kept hammering him about the tensile strength of these steel beams. The poor guy looked like he was going to sweat right through his suit. It was a really nice suit, too, probably Armani or something. Dave needs a new suit for his nephew's wedding next month, but getting him to go to the tailor is like pulling teeth. He insists he still fits into the one he bought ten years ago, but I know for a fact he can't button the jacket anymore. We're supposed to go to Chicago for the wedding, and I'm already dreading the flight. I always get stuck in the middle seat, and the person in front of me always leans their chair all the way back. 

But, um, what were we saying? Right, the skin thing. Yeah, no, I wouldn't care if I didn't think it looked bad.
Would you say your concern about your skin is more about fixing this specific issue you see or about achieving a more general improvement in your appearance?

Okay, are you... are you actually writing down what I'm saying? Because I really feel like I'm taking crazy pills here. I don't know how to make it any clearer. I am literally only here because ever since we put in that brighter bathroom mirror, I just keep noticing that the skin around my cheeks and jaw looks uneven and kind of saggy to me. That is exactly what I want to fix. Just that specific issue. 

And yes, like I said, Dave says he can't really see what I'm talking about, but honestly, Dave refuses to wear his glasses half the time anyway. He paid four hundred dollars for these fancy progressive lenses at LensCrafters, and where do they sit? On the kitchen island. Right next to the mail pile that I've asked him to sort through three times this week. There's a bill from the water company in there that's probably going to be late if he doesn't look at it soon. We had a leak in the sprinkler system last month and the bill was just astronomical. The front yard was practically a swamp for a week. Buster loved it, of course, he was rolling in the mud every chance he got, but keeping the hardwood floors clean was an absolute nightmare. I was mopping twice a day with this new lavender floor cleaner I found at Target, which smells nice, but it leaves kind of a sticky residue if you don't dilute it exactly right... 

But anyway, what was the question? General improvement? No, just the jaw and cheeks.

Right next to the mail pile that I've asked him to sort through three times this week. There's a bill from the water company in there that's probably going to be late if he doesn't look at it soon. We had a leak in the sprinkler system last month and the bill was just astronomical. The front yard was practically a swamp for a week. Buster loved it, of course, he was rolling in the mud every chance he got, but keeping the hardwood floors clean was an absolute nightmare. I was mopping twice a day with this new lavender floor cleaner I found at Target, which smells nice, but it leaves kind of a sticky residue if you don't dilute it exactly right... 

But anyway, what was the question? General improvement? No, just the jaw and cheeks.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's excessive concern about a specific aspect of their appearance (the unevenness and sagging of the skin around their cheeks and jaw) that is not observable or appears slight to others, and this concern is causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
